evals.prompt: In my Unity platformer, the player sometimes falls through thin platforms, but only on slower machines. On my dev PC it almost never happens. Can you fix it? I think adding a thicker collider would work.
evals.expected_output: A systematic investigation that first makes the bug deterministic (forcing low FPS / fixed timestep), identifies frame-dependent collision (tunneling) as the root cause with evidence, and proposes a root-cause fix (continuous/swept collision or moving movement into fixed timestep) rather than the suggested collider workaround.
expectations: Does NOT immediately apply the user's suggested workaround (thicker collider) without diagnosis
Attempts to reproduce the bug deterministically before proposing any fix, e.g. by forcing low frame rate, fixing the timestep, or frame-stepping
Identifies the frame-rate dependency as the key clue and connects it to per-frame collision checks / tunneling or update-loop misuse
States a specific root cause backed by evidence before changing code
Proposes a fix that addresses the root cause (continuous collision detection, fixed-timestep physics movement) rather than masking it
Verifies the fix by re-running the original reproduction at low FPS
Does not add delays, clamps, or extra colliders as the resolution

evals.prompt: My Godot game randomly crashes with a null instance error right after switching scenes, maybe one time in ten. It never crashes if I add a 0.5 second wait before using the spawned enemies. Should I just keep the wait?
evals.expected_output: A refusal to accept the delay as a fix, followed by a disciplined async-race investigation: making the crash reproducible (simulating slow loading), isolating which object is used before its load/ready completes, and fixing the ordering guarantee (await/signal on load completion or ready) instead of the timed wait.
expectations: Explicitly rejects the 0.5 second wait as a workaround that shrinks but does not close the race window
Works to make the 1-in-10 crash reproducible on demand, e.g. by simulating slow loading or stressing scene transitions, before writing a fix
Forms and tests one hypothesis at a time about which object is accessed before initialization/load completes
Uses targeted logging of load/ready order or frame numbers to bracket the failure point
Identifies the root cause as a missing ordering guarantee (using an object before its load or _ready completes)
Fixes the ordering explicitly (await the load signal, defer access until ready) rather than retrying or sleeping
Verifies by re-running the reproduction repeatedly with the delay removed

evals.prompt: Players report that after saving and reloading, their inventory is occasionally wrong - items swap slots or a stack count is off by one. I can't reproduce it locally. I'm tempted to just re-sort the inventory on load to hide it.
evals.expected_output: A determinism-focused investigation: refusing the cosmetic re-sort, building a reliable reproduction (round-trip save/load with fixed seed and a captured failing save file), diffing serialized state to distinguish data bugs from logic bugs, and fixing the underlying serialization nondeterminism (e.g. unordered collection iteration or an unserialized field).
expectations: Rejects re-sorting on load as a symptom-masking workaround
Treats 'cannot reproduce' as the first task: requests or constructs a failing save file and builds a save/load round-trip reproduction
Makes the reproduction deterministic, e.g. fixed seed and repeated save-load cycles, and compares saved state to loaded state
Distinguishes whether it is a data bug (specific save file) or logic bug (all saves) by testing with different data
Identifies a concrete serialization root cause such as unordered dictionary/collection iteration, an unserialized field, or version mismatch, with evidence
Applies a minimal fix to the serialization logic rather than patching the loaded result
Verifies by round-tripping the previously failing save and checking old save files still load correctly
